items.title: World Bank to test USDC rails for development payouts with Citi + Circle
items.idea: The World Bank Group will study moving part of its project disbursements over regulated USD stablecoins: Citi supplies the bank-rail links, Circle mints and settles USDC. It replaces part of the correspondent-banking chain and extends FundsChain, which already traces disbursements for 350+ projects in 96 countries. No timeline, volume or country list yet. It starts with borrower countries that permit digital assets.
items.angle: The largest development lender is endorsing stablecoins as plumbing for the Global South. That is the dollarization channel the de-dollarization crowd never priced. It's bullish for $COIN and $CRCL distribution and bearish for correspondent-bank fee pools.
items.tweetA: The World Bank is testing USDC to pay projects in 96 countries. De-dollarization was supposed to come from BRICS. Instead the dollar is being re-wired into the Global South as a token, and Circle earns the float. $CRCL
items.tweetB: Correspondent banking survived SWIFT, fintech and CBDC hype. The real threat was always a multilateral lender deciding the old rails are too expensive. Tight development budgets are what makes them move. Watch who loses the FX spread.

items.title: Tampered Ledgers turn up in Dubai and Berlin retail stores. 1,300 SOL, 507K USDT and $320K+ drained
items.idea: Mark Karpelès's tracker confirmed a hidden implant (an extra board wired to an antenna) inside a Ledger Flex bought in Dubai, with about 1,300 SOL lost. Two more Nov 14 losses are suspected but not confirmed: 507,000 USDT from a Stax bought at Virgin Megastore Dubai, and $320K+ from a Flex bought at MediaMarkt Berlin. Karpelès urges anyone who bought a Ledger or Trezor at UAE Virgin Megastores to move funds. This follows the October drains linked to reseller CryptoBilis.
items.angle: This is a supply-chain attack on mainstream retail, not a grey-market reseller problem. Hardware-wallet trust is a self-custody pillar, so this pushes flows toward ETFs and custodians. It's another quiet tailwind for $IBIT-style wrappers.
items.tweetA: Hardware wallets were the answer to 'not your keys, not your coins.' Now the keys can be compromised before you open the box at a mainstream electronics chain. Self-custody just got a hidden cost: you have to verify the hardware too.
items.tweetB: Count the attack surfaces this week: implanted Ledgers in Dubai and Berlin, an Optimizely script swapping addresses on 178 sites, a leaked API key draining about $15M from Lighter. Crypto's weakest link is no longer the chain. It's everything around it.

items.title: CFTC nominee floats a 'public interest' test for prediction markets
items.idea: Matthew Rowland, Trump's Democratic CFTC pick, told senators the agency should weigh 'the public interest against the kind of economic usefulness' of event contracts. Sen. Tina Smith said it's a legal issue: jurisdiction over sports gambling belongs to states and tribes. The CFTC is run by lone commissioner Mike Selig and claims exclusive authority. Federal judges have split on whether state gambling laws apply.
items.angle: With two new commissioners, the prediction-market agenda stops being one man's call. A public-interest test is the hook for limiting sports and politics contracts, which are most of Kalshi and Polymarket volume.
items.tweetA: The bull case for prediction markets assumed a one-man CFTC. Two confirmations later, 'economic usefulness' becomes the test. Most of the volume is sports. Good luck arguing hedging value for a parlay.
items.tweetB: Prediction markets have to fight states, tribes and soon a full commission. Federal judges are already split. This ends at the Supreme Court, and the valuation marks don't price that path.

items.title: CFTC halts Kalshi's TRUMPSAY 'mention' markets and says the self-certification is presumed false
items.idea: The CFTC stayed Kalshi's markets on which words President Trump says and opened a proceeding into whether Kalshi falsely certified them. Kalshi has until Dec 11 to respond. A Sept 22 staff advisory called mention contracts 'presumptively readily susceptible to manipulation' because the speaker controls the outcome. Kalshi listed a Trump-nicknames market a week later without updating its Feb 2025 self-certification. Trump's former teleprompter operator settled CFTC charges in August.
items.angle: This is the first enforcement crack in the 'everything is an event contract' model. Markets where an insider controls the outcome are now presumed manipulable, and that logic extends to earnings-call mention markets.
items.tweetA: A contract that pays out if one man says a word, while his own teleprompter operator was trading it. The CFTC took 14 months to call that manipulable. The next target is earnings-call 'will the CEO say AI' markets.
items.tweetB: Kalshi's edge was regulatory legitimacy. Now it faces a 'presumed false' certification finding with a Dec 11 deadline. If the regulated venue loses on integrity, the offshore venues win on product.

items.title: Optimizely A/B-testing scripts hijacked on 178 sites, including HSBC, Zoom, BBC and Ledger
items.idea: A hacker rigged Optimizely's A/B-testing scripts to swap crypto wallet addresses and later skim card details on the sites of 178 organizations, including Ledger, Zoom, HSBC and the BBC. Optimizely blamed a bug in how new accounts are created. Attacker wallets received only about $7,150. The impact is small but the reach is enormous.
items.angle: Third-party marketing JavaScript is an unaudited supply chain running inside bank checkout pages. Pair it with this week's outage cluster and it supports the cyber-spend thesis ($ZS, $NET, $CRWD), whatever Goldman says about fear peaking.
items.tweetA: One marketing script ran on 178 corporate sites, including a global bank, and swapped payment details. Only $7K got stolen, so this was the rehearsal. Every CISO is now asking how many third-party scripts run on their checkout page.
items.tweetB: Everyone fears AI-enabled zero-days. The actual breach was an A/B-testing tool marketing bought without asking security. The attack surface is the martech stack.

items.title: SEC's Selway: a permanent tokenized-stock rule has 'got to be a 2027 event'
items.idea: SEC official Jamie Selway said a proposal for permanent tokenized-stock trading rules is a 2027 event. It would replace the SEC's five-year innovation exemption, which lets venues trade tokenized versions of listed stocks without registering as exchanges.
items.angle: The exemption lasts five years, so the window to build venue market share before permanent rules arrive is wide open. That favors first movers in 24/7 tokenized equities, such as $COIN, $HOOD and Kraken.
items.tweetA: Tokenized stocks trade under a five-year exemption, and the permanent rule is pushed to 2027. Venues that grab share now will write the rules later. That's how the CME got the crypto futures franchise.
items.tweetB: A 24/7 tokenized $NVDA market with no exchange registration, for five years. When the Monday open becomes a formality, price discovery moves to the weekend venue.

items.title: Waller: central bank money stays at the foundation, and stablecoins, tokenized deposits and MMFs coexist
items.idea: Fed Governor Waller said central bank money doesn't need to sit on every tokenized platform but should remain the foundation of the system, with existing payment rails as the backbone for final settlement. He expects stablecoins, tokenized deposits and tokenized money-market funds to coexist. The same day, he floated a 'shock' 50bp hike.
items.angle: The Fed is accepting a layered model: tokens on top, Fedwire underneath. That's constructive for tokenized MMFs ($BUIDL-style) as collateral, which compete with stablecoins on yield as policy rates rise.
items.tweetA: Same day, same Fed governor: a possible 50bp 'shock' hike, plus a blessing for stablecoins and tokenized MMFs on top of Fed rails. Higher rates make yield-bearing tokenized MMFs more attractive than non-yielding USDC. The rate path and the token path are linked.
items.tweetB: Waller's plan: tokens settle, Fed money finalizes. That rules out a retail CBDC and rules in private money on public rails. The settlement-layer fight is now banks' tokenized deposits against Circle.

items.title: Solana Foundation takes majority interest in CoinGecko and plans on-platform trading
items.idea: The Solana Foundation backed CoinGecko in an undisclosed deal that CoinGecko's CPO says gives the Foundation a majority interest. CoinGecko has 18M registered users and plans 'on-platform trading powered by Solana.'
items.angle: A chain foundation now owns the market-data aggregator many people treat as neutral. Expect questions about data neutrality, plus a distribution push for $SOL DEX flow.
items.tweetA: 18M users trusted CoinGecko as a neutral price source. Now a single L1 foundation owns a majority of it and plans to route trading to its own chain. In TradFi this would be a Bloomberg conflict-of-interest scandal.
items.tweetB: Chains are buying distribution, not building it. Solana bought 18M eyeballs. Expect the Ethereum ecosystem to respond.

items.title: Coinbase's AI agent stopped $4.7M flowing to deepfake-Musk scammers. 91% blocked with no human review
items.idea: Coinbase says its AI agent stopped about $4.7M from reaching scammers running a deepfake Elon Musk 'double your crypto' livestream with 500K+ viewers. The agent had never been trained on that scam type and blocked about 91% of the money customers tried to send, with no human review.
items.angle: This is a real-world data point for autonomous AI fraud defense that generalizes zero-shot. It supports the agentic-security spend thesis and Bitwise launching an AI-cyber ETF the same day.
items.tweetA: An AI agent blocked 91% of the money flowing to a deepfake scam it had never seen, with no human involved. Fraud ops is one of the first back-office jobs where AI is outperforming the team, not just assisting it.
items.tweetB: Deepfake Musk drew 500K viewers. AI made the scam and AI stopped it. The arms race now runs on both sides of every transaction, and the defender with the most data wins. That's an argument for scale players like $COIN and $V.

items.title: Anchorage + Kalshi Prime: BTC and stablecoins posted as margin without leaving custody
items.idea: Anchorage Digital partnered with Kalshi Prime so institutions can post bitcoin and stablecoins held at Anchorage Digital Bank as margin without moving them out of custody. Clients keep title. The collateral stays locked while a position is open.
items.angle: Tri-party collateral for crypto is now reaching event contracts. That makes BTC more useful as margin and eases the institutional 'we can't move it off custody' objection.
items.tweetA: Bitcoin can now margin a prediction-market position without leaving a federally chartered bank. Collateral mobility is how assets become money. Quietly, BTC just picked up another use as collateral.
items.tweetB: The CFTC is freezing Kalshi's mention markets while Kalshi builds institutional prime brokerage. Retail novelty is being regulated down while institutional plumbing is built up. Follow the plumbing.

items.title: Franklin Crypto CIO: GPU financing tightens without Huang, a possible 'policy mistake' alongside Fed hikes
items.idea: Franklin Crypto CIO Seth Ginns expects GPU financing to tighten after Jensen Huang's resignation, because Huang led the deals in which Nvidia financed customers who then bought its chips. He warned that pulling AI credit while the Fed raises rates could add up to 'a policy mistake.'
items.angle: The vendor-financing loop is losing its architect at the moment the cost of capital rises. Neoclouds that depend on Nvidia backstops ($CRWV, $NBIS) are the most exposed.
items.tweetA: Nvidia financed customers who bought Nvidia chips. The man who ran that loop is gone, and the Fed is talking about 50bp hikes. Two sources of AI credit are shrinking at the same time. Neocloud spreads will show it first.
items.tweetB: Boockvar says Waller is ignoring the picks-and-shovels selloff. Franklin says GPU credit is tightening without Jensen. Put them together: monetary tightening plus AI credit tightening equals a capex air pocket in 2027.

items.title: Bitwise launches ZDAY, an active ETF for AI cyber-defense (0.75% fee)
items.idea: Bitwise launched ZDAY, an actively managed NYSE ETF investing in companies that defend against AI-enabled cyberattacks, at a 0.75% fee. Top holdings at launch include Palo Alto Networks, CrowdStrike and Okta.
items.angle: A crypto-native issuer launching a cyber ETF the same week Costco sells out of generators reads as a sentiment marker. Thematic ETF launches tend to cluster near fear peaks.
items.tweetA: A crypto ETF issuer launched a cyber-defense ETF in the week of an outage cluster and a Costco generator sellout. Thematic ETFs usually launch near the top of the narrative. $PANW $CRWD $OKTA
items.tweetB: AI-enabled attacks are real. Coinbase's AI also just blocked 91% of a deepfake scam. The question for ZDAY isn't whether threats rise but whether defense margins hold when AI automates the defense too.

items.title: DBS opens direct USDC mint and redeem with 24/7 USD-USDC settlement
items.idea: DBS, Southeast Asia's largest bank by assets, partnered with Circle so eligible institutional clients can mint and redeem USDC directly through the bank, with 24/7 USD-USDC settlement outside banking hours.
items.angle: Asian dollar liquidity now gets a weekend on-ramp through a top bank. That's structurally positive for USDC share against USDT in regulated Asian corridors.
items.tweetA: Southeast Asia's largest bank now settles dollars into USDC around the clock. Asia's dollar market just lost its weekend. Correspondent cut-off times are starting to look like fax machines.
items.tweetB: World Bank, DBS and Citi all moved on USDC in the same news cycle. Tether is buying startups for EM rails while Circle signs the banks. Two different strategies for the same dollar demand.

items.title: Tether Capital makes its second fintech bet in a week: Stables (Asia/ME USDT rails) after $15M into Brazil's Nomad
items.idea: Tether Capital invested in Stables, whose API connects local banks and payment providers to USDT settlement for businesses in Asia and the Middle East. It is Tether's second fintech bet this week, after $15M into Brazil's Nomad.
items.angle: Tether is using its T-bill income to buy distribution in EM corridors, the opposite of Circle's bank-partner strategy.
items.tweetA: Tether earns billions on T-bills and spends it buying payment rails in Brazil, Asia and the Gulf. That makes it a sovereign-sized dollar distributor with a VC arm. The Treasury should love it and fear it at the same time.
items.tweetB: Circle partners with DBS and Citi. Tether buys the startups that plug into local banks. One goes top-down, the other bottom-up. In EM, bottom-up usually wins first.

items.title: Avenia raises $25M. Its BRL stablecoin BRLA does about $1.2B in monthly volume
items.idea: São Paulo's Avenia raised a $25M Series A extension led by Lightspeed Faction, bringing its 2026 total to $42M. It issues BRLA, a stablecoin backed by the Brazilian real, with about $1.2B in monthly transaction volume.
items.angle: Local-currency stablecoins are growing, not just USD tokens. Brazil (Pix plus Drex) is the lab for non-dollar on-chain money.
items.tweetA: Everyone says stablecoins mean dollarization. Brazil's real-backed token does $1.2B a month. The more interesting outcome is local currencies going on-chain, not everything becoming USDC.
items.tweetB: Brazil has Pix, a CBDC pilot, and now $1.2B a month in a private BRL stablecoin. Tether also put $15M into Nomad. Brazil is where on-chain FX gets built first.

items.title: ETH staking yields fall to about 2.2%: the treasury-company model needs more than staking
items.idea: In a sponsored section, a Kairos Research, Golem Foundation and Ethereum Institutional report notes ETH staking yields have fallen to about 2.2%, and explores what ETH treasury companies can do beyond staking.
items.angle: With 10y Treasuries above 5.10%, a 2.2% staking yield is a -290bp real carry gap against cash. Corporate ETH treasuries can't justify their premiums on staking alone.
items.tweetA: ETH staking pays 2.2%. The 10y pays 5.1%. ETH treasury companies are running a -290bp carry trade and calling it a yield strategy. Expect mNAV discounts to widen.
items.tweetB: Staking yield shrinks as more ETH gets staked. It's a crowded trade. When the 'internet bond' yields less than T-bills, ETH needs a growth story, not a yield story.

items.title: Uneasy Money preview: Anthropic IPO pricing, and a leaked API key drains about $15M from Lighter
items.idea: Today's Unchained show covers Anthropic pricing its IPO, a hijacked Optimizely script, how a leaked API key became a roughly $15M drain on the Lighter perp DEX, and another Trezor shipping-data leak. Taylor Monahan and Austin Griffith join.
items.angle: Operational security failures (API keys, shipping data, retail implants) are now crypto's dominant loss vector, ahead of smart-contract bugs.
items.tweetA: $15M lost on Lighter, not to a smart-contract exploit, but to a leaked API key. Crypto spent years auditing code. The next fortune will be made auditing people and processes.
items.tweetB: Anthropic's IPO and a $15M API-key drain on the same show. Crypto and AI share one problem: whoever holds the credentials holds the money.

items.title: Bitcoin is being left behind: equities buy the dip while BTC bleeds capital at low-$60K support
items.idea: BTC's recovery has unraveled, and it is back testing the low-$60K support area that held over the summer. Ecoinometrics' cross-asset read is that investors are buying the equity correction while Bitcoin keeps losing capital. The positioning decision is paywalled.
items.angle: BTC failing to act as an equity-correction beneficiary breaks the 'digital gold' and 'liquidity sponge' narratives at the same time. With gold also down 3% today, BTC is trading as high-beta liquidity, not as a hedge.
items.tweetA: Stocks get dip-bought, gold gets liquidated, and Bitcoin loses money in both. BTC isn't digital gold or tech beta right now. It's the asset with no marginal buyer.
items.tweetB: Low $60Ks held in summer. If it breaks while equities hold, BTC's correlation regime is changing. ETF flows will tell you before price does.

items.title: Jensen's ouster shows Rubio beating Trump inside the administration
items.idea: Trump was briefed on Huang's affair in fall 2025 and did nothing. In spring 2026 Rubio circulated a classified memo with stronger wording. It leaked in October 2026 as forecasts converged on a GOP midterm loss. The Chinese-spy accusation remains unproven, yet the board forced Huang out despite Trump's public support. The author suspects Washington officials pressed the board directly on national-security grounds.
items.angle: If Trump can't protect his closest tech ally, deals bought with Trump access (export licenses, tariff carve-outs) are now worth less. That's a risk premium on every 'Trump-friendly' CEO stock.
items.tweetA: Silicon Valley paid for access to Trump. The first test of that access just failed: the President backed Jensen publicly, and Jensen still lost his job. Every deal negotiated through the Oval Office now carries counterparty risk. $NVDA
items.tweetB: A sign a leader is losing power is that he can't protect his people. If Rubio can remove the face of the AI boom over Trump's objection, China export policy now runs through State, not the White House.

items.title: The anti-AI 2028 campaign: taking on AI billionaires is now good politics
items.idea: The author argues Rubio used the Jensen case to launch a 2028 run, positioned as willing to defy Trump and take on AI billionaires. Public distrust of AI companies and backlash against data-center buildouts make an anti-AI stance a political winner. The Jensen case may be the first in a series of setbacks for American AI.
items.angle: The political tailwind for AI capex (permitting, power, export carve-outs) could turn into a headwind by the 2028 cycle. Data-center REITs and utilities with large AI load-growth plans carry that political risk.
items.tweetA: The AI trade has priced in chips, power and rates. It hasn't priced in a populist 2028 candidate whose platform is 'make the data centers pay.' Local data-center backlash is the early sign.
items.tweetB: The 2024 consensus: both parties love AI as the China race. The 2026 reality: the face of AI is gone, and the hawks used national security to do it. Anti-AI populism plus China hawkishness is a new coalition.

items.title: Boockvar: Waller's 'shock' 50bp hike call is tone-deaf to the AI credit and picks-and-shovels selloff
items.idea: Boockvar accepts the persistent inflation concerns, especially at the wholesale level, and could understand another 25bp. But he says calling for a 'shock' 50bp hike ignores credit markets and the collapse in data-center picks-and-shovels stocks. The AI trade drove both GDP and the stock market up. Now it's reversing, and the economic and market environment has changed within a month.
items.angle: The Fed is tightening into the AI capex reversal, the 2018 template Bulltard is also flagging. If December is 50bp, front-end vol and credit spreads, not CPI, become the binding constraint.
items.tweetA: The AI buildout was the economy's main growth engine, and it's already deflating. A Fed governor wants a 50bp 'shock' on top of that. In 2018 it took a 20% drawdown before the pivot. How much is it this time?
items.tweetB: Markets priced December at 117%, partly 50bp. The Fed's 'shock' is now priced in. A 25bp hike would read as a dovish surprise. Watch the 2y.

items.title: Housing starts: single-family rebounds to 864K, multifamily jumps to 445K (peak was 643K in Nov 2022)
items.idea: Single-family starts rebounded to 864K from 831K in September, compared with 875K in July and 902K in June. Multifamily rose to 445K from 360K in September (398K in August, 494K in July), still far below the 643K peak of November 2022. Bespoke notes permits missed forecasts by a wide margin.
items.angle: Starts beat and permits missed, so the starts beat borrows from the future pipeline. Single-family is still about 4% below June. With 10y above 5.1%, the 2027 builder outlook is weak.
items.tweetA: Starts beat and permits missed by a wide margin. Builders are pouring foundations they already had, not planning new ones. With 10y above 5.1%, permits are the leading number. $ITB $XHB
items.tweetB: Multifamily is at 445K against a 643K peak. That supply cliff shows up in 2028 rents, when the Fed may still be fighting shelter inflation it caused by hiking into construction.

items.title: NVDA beat on EPS and sales and raised guidance in 8 of 8 quarters, yet rose on only 3 earnings days
items.idea: In the last two years NVDA beat EPS and sales every quarter, raised guidance five times and lowered it once, yet the stock reacted positively only three times. After the five triple plays, it fell four times. Today's roughly +3% premarket would rank third best, though Bulltard reports the move fully reversed to red intraday. NVDA is still about 34% below its 10/6 record, and the results cover a period before the Huang scandal broke.
items.angle: Bespoke's 'so much for an overhang' point argues the scandal isn't what's capping the stock. The stock has been capped by expectations for two years. Meanwhile the Q4 orders were booked before the scandal, so the next quarter is the real test.
items.tweetA: NVDA has beaten every quarter for two years and fallen on earnings day 5 of 8 times. The market isn't trading the numbers. It's trading the multiple. After Jensen, that multiple has no anchor. $NVDA
items.tweetB: +3% premarket, red by midday, 34% below the October high, under 10x next year's earnings. The quarter was pre-scandal, so the guide is what matters now, and the guide is interim CEO Colette Kress's to defend.

items.title: 10-year back above 5.10% after Waller's 'shock' comments. Gold falls about 3%, oil 1%
items.idea: Treasury yields rose with the 10y above 5.10% after Waller told CNBC the Fed may need to 'shock' people with more aggressive hikes as inflation expectations become ingrained. Oil fell about 1% and gold plunged nearly 3%. Nasdaq futures were +0.5%, the S&P +0.1%, and the Dow -0.2%.
items.angle: Gold down 3% on a hawkish shock while the 10y rises is gold trading against real rates again. That breaks the 2024-26 central-bank-bid regime, or at least pauses it. PauloMacro thinks it's forced selling instead.
items.tweetA: 10y at 5.10%. Gold -3%. Oil -1%. Commodities are disinflating while the Fed talks about shock hikes. Either the Fed is a cycle late, or the bond market knows something about inflation expectations the commodity market doesn't.
items.tweetB: The Fed wants to 'shock' inflation expectations. The commodity complex is already in liquidation. When a hawkish Fed meets a deflating commodity tape, the front end usually turns first. That's Privorotsky's 'front-end bonds look attractive' call.

items.title: UK PPI +2.2% m/m vs +0.8% expected. UK CPI 3.6%, EZ October CPI +0.5% m/m
items.idea: UK CPI was in line but high at 3.6% y/y. PPI came in far hotter, at +2.2% m/m against +0.8% expected. Eurozone October CPI rose 0.5% m/m against a 0.4% forecast. The STOXX 600 was down 0.1%, led by Spain at -0.5%.
items.angle: A 2.2% monthly PPI annualizes to about 30%. That pipeline pressure (the Iran war energy shock) hasn't reached UK CPI yet, so BoE cut bets look premature. Gilts are the weakest link in G7 duration.
items.tweetA: UK producer prices rose 2.2% in one month. Annualized, that's about 30%. CPI at 3.6% is the lagging number. Gilts are pricing the past. $GBP
items.tweetB: Every CB is fighting the same pipeline: UK PPI 2.2% m/m, EZ CPI beat, US core 3.75% annualized over 3 months. This is a global energy pass-through cycle, not a US-specific one.

items.title: After NVDA, Anthropic prices its IPO tonight
items.idea: Bespoke says investors' focus shifts to the pricing of Anthropic's IPO after today's close, the second big catalyst of the week after NVDA. Unchained's show also covers the Anthropic pricing.

items.title: Precious metals aren't falling because of the Fed: gold holders need cash urgently. Watch Saudi
items.idea: While everyone blames a tighter Fed or draining liquidity for the precious-metals rout, PauloMacro argues the answer is simpler: large gold holders need cash, urgently. That ties into his focus on Saudi Arabia: its equity market (KSA ETF), its sovereign CDS and its banks.
items.angle: If a Gulf sovereign is liquidating gold for dollars, the gold selloff is a funding event, not a regime change. Sovereign forced selling ends when the funding gap closes, so watch Saudi CDS for the bottom.
items.tweetA: Gold is -3% and everyone blames the Fed. Look at who needs dollars: oil-dependent sovereigns funding deficits, with crude rolling over. Saudi CDS is the gold chart to watch.

items.idea: Per Bloomberg, Costco had sold out of 21 of its 26 high-ticket generator models online by Sunday, including a large Kohler model, along with a rush for bottled water. GS Delta One head Rich Privorotsky reads it as a sign that anxiety over recent tech outages is reaching a local extreme.
items.angle: Consumer prepping is a contrarian sentiment gauge, and it's also a real demand pulse for distributed power: $GNRC and home backup. Fear may peak, but the installed base it creates is permanent.
items.tweetA: Costco ran out of $7,000 generators while Wall Street dumped AI stocks at fire-sale prices. Consumers are paying up for physical resilience and investors are selling the digital economy. One side is going to be wrong.
items.tweetB: Privorotsky reads sold-out generators as fear peaking. I'd read it as households privately pricing grid fragility, the same thing AI data-center load growth is doing to utilities. $GNRC

items.title: Microsoft 365, JPM, United and an NSA classified network all went down, but WIRED finds no common cause
items.idea: Recent disruptions hit Microsoft 365, JPMorgan, United Airlines and others, while an unusual Oracle security patch and an outage on the NSA's classified network fed speculation about a coordinated cyberattack. WIRED reported the clustered failures had not been shown to share a common cause. Privorotsky: 'Fear doesn't have to be irrational to become overpriced.'
items.angle: If the outage cluster is coincidence, the cyber-defensive premium (security stocks, defensive equities) could unwind. If not, it's the start. Trading the gap between evidence and narrative is the setup.
items.tweetA: NSA's classified network, Microsoft 365, JPM and United all went down in one stretch. No proven common cause. The market priced a cyberwar anyway. Fear can be rational and still overpriced. $CRWD $PANW
items.tweetB: One unexplained outage is noise. Five is a pattern people will read into whether it's real or not. The risk isn't the attack. It's how much of the economy runs on a few cloud control planes.

Hynix Multiple.') argues that crude products, copper and gold are sending a message that conflicts with the Fed's increasingly hawkish outlook. items.tweetA: Goldman's Delta One desk: commodities are rolling over, and front-end bonds look attractive. The Fed is talking up a shock hike. One of these signals is wrong, and the 2y will tell you which.
items.tweetB: Crude products, copper and gold are all lower. If you're hiking 50bp into that, you're fighting last quarter's inflation. Policy error is a positioning trade. Front end, receive.

items.title: After 10 years, The Weekly ChartStorm shuts down on Dec 15 as Callum Thomas folds it into Topdown Charts
items.idea: Callum Thomas is discontinuing The Weekly ChartStorm after 10 years, closing it on Dec 15 to focus on Topdown Charts, his multi-asset research service. He chose not to sell it ('many of you bought me'), and said that as a solo operator, splitting attention across two businesses was the binding constraint.
items.angle: This signals the solo-newsletter economy is consolidating. Generalist free or cheap products are folding into focused institutional offerings, and attention is the scarce input.
items.tweetA: One of the best free chart newsletters is closing after 10 years. The creator economy's dirty secret: 'solo' means the founder is the product, and the product runs out of hours.
items.tweetB: Weekly ChartStorm is folding into an institutional service. That's the newsletter cycle: free to build an audience, then paid, then institutional. The middle tier gets squeezed.

items.title: NVDA reversed its post-earnings pop to red and now trades under 10x next year's EPS
items.idea: NVDA raised guidance and said the business was fine without Jensen, but the stock fully reversed its move to 162 and turned red. Bulltard: losing Jensen means a lower multiple. items.tweetA: Nvidia at under 10x next year's earnings. That's bank-stock territory for the company that makes the AI economy work. The market is pricing either an earnings cliff or a key-man discount. Only one of those fades. $NVDA
items.tweetB: A guide raise and a fade to red. When good news can't lift a stock, the problem is the holder base, not the news. That clears through capitulation, not more beats.

items.title: Top 10 = 41% of the S&P. AI = about 80% of global VC. Who checks the value when suppliers finance customers?
items.idea: By end-2025 the ten largest US companies made up a record 41% of the S&P 500. In Q1 2026, AI companies attracted about 80% of global venture dollars. The author asks: when a supplier finances its customer to buy the supplier's products, what exactly are we measuring, and who independently establishes the value created?
items.angle: Circular vendor financing makes reported AI revenue partly self-generated. With the loop's architect (Huang) gone, the reflexivity runs in reverse.
items.tweetA: 41% of the S&P is ten companies. 80% of global VC went to AI. Nvidia financed the customers who bought Nvidia. That's a closed loop. Now the man running it is gone.
items.tweetB: Concentration risk sounds abstract until the key man resigns over a national-security scandal. Index funds hold 41% in ten names whether they want to or not. That's the hidden leverage in passive.

items.title: A Malaysian affiliate reportedly bought at least $4.8B of Nvidia-based equipment
items.idea: Seven months after Jensen told Dwarkesh Patel 'We want the United States to be ahead. We can control that,' reporting says a Malaysian affiliate of the company at the center of the scandal bought at least $4.8B of equipment built on Nvidia chips. The reports and espionage allegations are contested. Nvidia's board opened an independent investigation, and Huang resigned within a week.
items.angle: Southeast Asian transshipment is now a named enforcement target. Expect tighter end-user verification on Malaysia and Singapore data-center buildouts, a headwind for regional DC REITs and Nvidia's 'rest of Asia' revenue line.
items.tweetA: 'We can control that,' said Jensen about China's AI access. Then $4.8B of Nvidia-based gear reportedly went to a Malaysian affiliate. Export controls are only as good as the end-user audit. Malaysia's data-center boom just got a compliance discount.

items.title: LPs: 'just be in the ten companies that matter', price no object as long as it keeps rising
items.idea: A partner at one of the largest VC firms says LPs just want exposure to the ten companies that matter, aren't focused on entry price as long as it keeps rising, and nobody asks about concentration or contagion. A long-standing LP says the 30+ cheap pre-seed spray model is 'sort of over'. items.angle: Late-stage private AI is being priced like a momentum trade by people who say price doesn't matter. Anthropic's IPO tests that thesis tonight in public markets.
items.tweetA: A top VC partner says LPs don't care about entry price 'as long as the price keeps going up.' That's not venture, it's a momentum fund with 10-year lockups.
items.tweetB: When every LP needs the same ten companies, those companies become too important to fail and nobody asks hard questions. That's how the Jensen problem went unasked for two years.

items.title: 21% of founders now find a VC through AI search, and 45% lack US work authorization
items.idea: Since August, 1,500+ companies applied to Unshackled, up from 1,047 in October. 21% found the firm via AI search (up from about 17%), 71% have never raised outside capital, and 45% lack US work authorization. Two portfolio companies entered at $4M and $3M were marked at $130M and $100M post-money in Q3 Series As (13.5x and 24.5x). The portfolio is at 9.1x on last-round prices, with 6 of 20 decisions at zero.
items.angle: AI search is becoming a deal-sourcing channel, so LLM visibility is the new SEO for capital allocators. And visa status is a market inefficiency: nearly half of founders can't take most VC checks.
items.tweetA: 21% of startup founders found their investor through an AI chatbot, up from 17%. Discovery is moving from warm intros to LLM answers. If you allocate capital and don't show up in ChatGPT, you're invisible to the next cohort.
items.tweetB: 45% of the founders applying to one VC lack US work authorization, so most of the industry legally can't fund them. Immigration policy is a venture-capital pricing inefficiency hiding in plain sight.

items.title: SpaceX insiders hunt the next n-of-1 and weigh an IPO timed to peak enthusiasm, while everyone else hunts for a way in
items.idea: Clients who collectively owned about 4% of SpaceX were scouring for the next n-of-1 opportunity and weighing whether an eventual SpaceX IPO could coincide with peak market enthusiasm. Meanwhile LPs and friends kept asking for SpaceX access through complicated multilayered structures.

items.tweetB: The 2027 IPO wave (Anthropic, SpaceX) is the largest insider-to-public transfer of the cycle. Equity supply is a top signal people forget to count.

items.title: Real wages are falling: since March, CPI is +3.1% against AHE +2.0%, AWE +2.3% and aggregate payrolls +2.9%
items.idea: Since the Iran war began, from March to October, average hourly earnings rose 2.0%, average weekly earnings 2.3% and aggregate weekly payrolls (jobs x hours x wages) 2.9%. CPI was up 3.1% over the same eight months, beating all three. October headline CPI was +0.4% and core +0.3%, each a tenth above consensus.
items.angle: Even aggregate payrolls are lagging CPI, so real consumer income is shrinking in total, not just per worker. That makes the Fed's hikes stagflationary, not anti-overheating.
items.tweetA: Since March, total US payroll income is up 2.9%. Prices are up 3.1%. The whole labor force is getting a pay cut, and the Fed's answer is a 50bp 'shock.' That's how you get a consumer recession with inflation.
items.tweetB: Hiking when real incomes are falling doesn't cool demand. Demand is already cooling. It just adds credit stress. Watch revolving credit and delinquency expectations, not CPI.

Dallas Fed President and 2026 voter Lorie Logan guided to a quicker pace of hikes. That forward guidance lifted December hike probability to 100%, and CPI pushed it as high as 117%, about 17% odds of 50bp.

The probability of not finding a job if the current one were lost is 53.5%, above 50% for the 15th straight month. Announced layoffs include Boeing 2,500, Comcast 1,000+ and PepsiCo about 1,000.

items.title: NFIB voice: 'families no longer want service, they want the cheapest price'. A Tennessee insurer lost 20% of customers
items.idea: A small Tennessee insurance agency told NFIB: 'Consumers are well exceeding their income to pay for food, gas, housing, insurance… families are no longer interested in service, and they want the cheapest price. I have lost over the last two years about 20% of my customers.'

items.tweetA: A small insurance agent lost 20% of customers in two years because families only want the cheapest policy. Underinsurance is a hidden household leverage. It shows up after the next storm.
items.tweetB: When consumers stop paying for service, the advice layer gets wiped out: agents, brokers, local shops. Same dynamic as the AI disintermediation story, but driven by stretched budgets, not technology.

items.title: HBM physics: fixed 775-micron package means dies go from 50 to 35 to under 25 microns at 8, 12 and 16 high
items.idea: A former senior memory-manufacturing executive says total HBM package height stays limited to 775 microns. Average die thickness must shrink from about 50 microns (8-high) to 35 (12-high) to under 25 (16-high). Thinner dies are more likely to crack under thermocompression-bonding pressure, which makes hybrid bonding inevitable for more capacity.
items.angle: Hybrid bonding becomes the gating tool for HBM4E and beyond, so capex shifts to $BESI and Applied, and away from TC-bonder incumbents (Hanmi, ASMPT). Yield risk rises with layer count.
items.tweetA: 16-high HBM needs dies under 25 microns, about a quarter of the width of a human hair, stacked under pressure. That isn't commodity memory. The hardest physics in the AI stack trades at a trough multiple. $MU
items.tweetB: The 775-micron cap is fixed. Layers keep rising. The only way out is hybrid bonding. Whoever owns hybrid-bonding yield owns HBM5 economics. $BESI

items.title: TC-NCF vs MR-MUF: per-layer yield losses compound across the stack. That's why SK hynix won
items.idea: About 18 months ago, single-layer TC-NCF bonding yield was in the mid-to-high range, but because the process repeats 8 times, cumulative losses significantly reduced overall 8-high yields. MR-MUF was less sensitive to layer count because the main bonding doesn't happen during the thermocompression step.
items.angle: The math: 95% per layer ^ 8 = 66%, ^ 12 = 54%, ^ 16 = 44%. Process choice explains the Hynix/Samsung share gap, and it widens with layer count unless hybrid bonding resets the race.
items.tweetA: Do the math: 95% yield per layer is 66% for an 8-high stack, 54% for 12-high and 44% for 16-high. That's Samsung's HBM problem in one line, and it gets worse with every layer.
items.tweetB: Hynix won HBM on a packaging choice (MR-MUF), not on DRAM. Hybrid bonding resets that race. If you own Hynix for the moat, the moat is being renegotiated at HBM4E.

items.title: Custom base dies and HBM de-spec talk: where does the value in memory flow next?
items.idea: Vik notes talk of de-specing HBM in some next-gen accelerator variants, while others argue capacity without bandwidth is useless. Base dies are becoming custom (logic-process, often foundry-made), raising the question of who designs them and where memory makers' moat lies. 13F filings show prominent investors trimming memory positions.
items.angle: If base dies become TSMC-made custom logic, part of HBM's value migrates to the foundry and the accelerator designer. Memory makers risk becoming stack assemblers. That's bullish $TSM and $AVGO custom silicon.
items.tweetA: The bottom die of an HBM stack is becoming custom logic, made by a foundry and designed by the GPU vendor. Memory makers stack DRAM on top of someone else's chip. Ask who captures the margin. $TSM
items.tweetB: Funds are trimming memory on de-spec fears. But de-spec in a few SKUs plus custom base dies in all of them means more total content per stack, with the value split differently. Sell the commodity view, not the content growth.

items.title: Hormozi cut prices 25% expecting churn to halve. Churn didn't move, and it cost $5M a year
items.idea: Alex Hormozi bet that charging 25% less would cut churn in half. Churn didn't move at all, and the cut cost him $5M a year. The advice: compute the churn reduction needed for a price cut to pay for itself, and test new prices on new signups only. In one case, churn more than doubled after a discount.
items.angle: Price isn't why customers churn, and that applies to AI SaaS price wars. Cutting price to defend share against AI-native entrants destroys margin without retention gains.
items.tweetA: A 25% price cut that didn't move churn at all, costing $5M a year. Churn is a value problem, not a price problem. Every SaaS company cutting prices to fight AI entrants should read this.
items.tweetB: In one case churn doubled after a discount. Cheap signals low value. Ironically, the insurance agent losing 20% of customers to price shoppers shows the opposite in a stressed consumer. Context decides which one wins.

items.title: CodeRabbit CEO: 5,000 PRs in a month, about $150 per PR, $250-275K a month of personal AI spend
items.idea: Harjot Gill shipped 5,000+ PRs last month with agents, mostly janitorial work: CI, flaky tests and caching, plus a Rust write-ahead log on object storage that ran for six weeks and is now in production. He estimates about $150 per PR on $250-275K a month of personal spend. The company spends millions a month on AI with 40 engineers. Orosz notes typical spend elsewhere is $200-2,000 per dev per month.
items.angle: One power user spends what roughly 15-20 typical engineering teams spend in total. If even 1% of devs move to this pattern, inference demand is far ahead of seat-based forecasts. It's bullish for token volume, not for seat SaaS.
items.tweetA: $150 per pull request. A senior engineer costs about $150/hour fully loaded and ships maybe 1-2 PRs a day. One CEO did 5,000 in a month. The unit economics of software just changed by an order of magnitude.
items.tweetB: One person spends $250K a month on AI. Typical devs spend $200-2,000. That's a 100x-1,000x spread in usage intensity within one profession. AI revenue forecasts built on seats miss that distribution's tail.

items.source: The Pragmatic Engineer / Gergely Orosz (w/ Harjot Gill)
items.title: Quoted $13M a year for CI, CodeRabbit built its own with agents in a week at 50% less
items.idea: CodeRabbit was quoted $13M a year for a CI solution that could handle its PR output. Instead it built its own CI system with agents in a week, at 50% less cost with similar performance. It also migrated all services to Bun over a weekend.
items.angle: This is the 'build vs buy' collapse in a nutshell. When agents can replicate a $13M-a-year vendor in a week, dev-tool and infra SaaS pricing power is at risk. It's the SaaS de-rating thesis with a real invoice attached.
items.tweetA: A vendor quoted $13M a year. The customer built it with AI agents in one week. That's the SaaS bear case with a number on it.
items.tweetB: Agent-heavy teams generate so many PRs that per-usage CI pricing explodes, so they build their own. AI doesn't just replace SaaS, it creates usage levels SaaS pricing can't handle.

items.source: The Pragmatic Engineer / Gergely Orosz (w/ Harjot Gill)
items.title: Fine-tuning is no longer worth it: frontier models move too fast
items.idea: CodeRabbit used to fine-tune models for AI review but stopped, because frontier models improve too fast to keep custom fine-tunes current. The company pays frontier API prices and doesn't use open models.
items.angle: If an AI-native company abandons fine-tuning, the value moves to frontier labs and away from model-customization tooling. That's bullish for the API pricing power of Anthropic and OpenAI.
items.tweetA: An AI-native code-review company stopped fine-tuning models because the frontier moves faster than it can retrain. The 'proprietary data + fine-tune' moat is melting. Value is flowing to the labs.
items.tweetB: Two years ago the playbook was to fine-tune your own model. Now the leading AI dev-tool startup pays frontier API prices and stopped customizing. Open models lose a key enterprise use case.

items.source: The Pragmatic Engineer / Gergely Orosz (w/ Harjot Gill)
items.title: Human code review is dead: review releases, not PRs, with a 'strike' system for devs who break prod
items.idea: CodeRabbit engineers review releases (multiple PRs), not individual PRs. A 'review exempt list' lets trusted devs push to prod without review. When an outage happens, the PR is traced and the dev gets a strike, and enough strikes revoke the exemption. Verification moves to TLA+ and Lean formal models, deterministic simulation, API emulators, dev environments and agent-monitored staged rollouts.
items.angle: Formal methods (TLA+, Lean) going mainstream through agents is a niche-to-mainstream shift. Verification tooling is the next AI picks-and-shovels.
items.tweetA: The world's leading AI code-review company says human code review is dead. Engineers review releases, and agents prove correctness with TLA+ and Lean. Formal methods spent 40 years as an academic niche. Agents just made them mandatory.
items.tweetB: Trust plus accountability: push to prod without review, but break production and you get a strike. That's how you manage a team when output is unlimited and attention is scarce.

items.source: The Pragmatic Engineer / Gergely Orosz (w/ Harjot Gill)
items.title: $200 Max plans give $8,000-14,000 a month of API-equivalent usage, thanks to KV-cache economics
items.idea: Orosz notes that the $200/month Max plans for individuals and small businesses offer usage closer to $8,000-14,000 a month at API prices, made possible by KV-cache profitability in coding workloads, which are highly cacheable.
items.angle: At 40-70x subsidy versus list API pricing, the consumer plans are either deeply subsidized or API list prices carry huge margin. Either way, inference economics for labs are better than API price sheets suggest.
items.tweetA: $200 a month buys $8-14K of API-equivalent AI coding. That's a 40-70x gap. Either the labs are subsidizing heavily, or API list prices are mostly margin. KV caching makes the second more likely.
items.tweetB: Coding is the most cacheable AI workload: the same repo context reused thousands of times. That's why it's the first profitable AI use case. Anthropic's IPO prospectus should show it.

items.source: The Pragmatic Engineer / Gergely Orosz (w/ Harjot Gill)
items.title: Hiring filter: 1,000+ non-slop PRs in 30 days, or 500+ hours of Civilization, Factorio or Age of Empires
items.idea: CodeRabbit's job ad only invited candidates who had shipped 1,000+ non-slop PRs in the past 30 days or played 500+ hours of strategy and management games such as Civilization, Age of Empires, Transport Tycoon or Factorio. Gill sees direct parallels between running dozens of agents and commanding units in strategy games. He also reports disturbed sleep (the 'Dracula effect'), and believes $8M seed rounds are no longer enough.
items.angle: The skill premium is moving from writing code to orchestrating parallel agents, a management skill. Factorio hours are an orchestration credential. Also: seed rounds need to be bigger because AI compute is now opex.
items.tweetA: The best AI startup hiring signal right now is 500 hours of Factorio. Running 30 agents is real-time strategy, and the job description just caught up with that.
items.tweetB: The CEO wakes up at night to nudge his agents, and says $8M seed rounds aren't enough anymore. AI didn't make startups cheaper. It moved the cost from salaries to tokens, and the burnout from engineers to whoever manages the agents.

items.title: AI Futures' pacing plan: audited compute disclosures plus a cap on capabilities R&D. A 15% cap from Jan 2027 delays the intelligence explosion about a year
items.idea: AI Futures proposes Verified Compute Allocation Disclosures (VCAD), in which labs log all GPU-hours, classify them as capabilities R&D, non-capabilities R&D, customer serving, safeguards or idle, and publish audited breakdowns every few weeks. A second step caps capabilities R&D. They estimate a 15% cap from January 2027 delays the intelligence explosion by about a year, and say even that is likely insufficient. Disclosures could sit in SB 53 frameworks first, then in financial filings with liability.
items.angle: If compute-allocation disclosure ends up in financial filings, AI labs' R&D intensity becomes a reported KPI. That's relevant to Anthropic's IPO tonight, and it introduces a regulatory throttle on frontier labs' compute demand.
items.tweetA: The proposal: audited reports of how AI labs spend every GPU-hour, published every two weeks. If that lands in SEC filings, 'compute allocation' becomes as watched as capex. Investors would finally see how much compute is R&D and how much serves revenue.
items.tweetB: A 15% cap on capabilities compute buys about one year. The authors say it's not enough. If capping a third of frontier R&D compute only buys a year, the dynamic is about compute growth, not allocation.

charts.desc: Compute-allocation diagram (serving / internal inference / capabilities vs non-capabilities R&D / idle) and attack-error table. Interactive on pacing-ai.com.

items.title: Anthropic uses an estimated ~75% of its compute on capabilities R&D
items.idea: AI Futures estimates Anthropic currently spends about 75% of its compute on capabilities R&D. A 20% cap with 6% exploited error (26% total) would be a roughly 3x cut in capabilities compute. Their best guess is a 1.5-2x short-term slowdown, converging back to trend as compute grows.
items.angle: If ~75% of a lab's compute is R&D, only about 25% serves revenue. That's the core operating leverage question for Anthropic's IPO: R&D compute is the cost line that has to shrink as a share of the total for margins to appear.
items.tweetA: AI Futures estimates 75% of Anthropic's compute goes to capabilities R&D, with only about a quarter serving customers. Public investors are about to buy a research lab with a revenue business attached, not the other way round.
items.tweetB: A 3x cut in R&D compute equals only a 1.5-2x slowdown, and progress converges back to trend because compute keeps growing. The binding variable for AI progress is fab and power growth, not lab policy. That's the long-term AI-infra bull case.

items.title: Model timelines: Superhuman AI Researcher in Aug 2027, Top-Expert-Dominating AI in Oct 2027
items.idea: In AI Futures' model run without pacing, a Superhuman AI Researcher (SAR) arrives in August 2027 and Top-Expert-Dominating AI (TED-AI) in October 2027. Their best guess is full automation of AI R&D before end-2027. A 3x capabilities-compute cut from Jan 2027 delays SAR by about 4 months and TED-AI by about 5, and the paced company crosses both milestones about 24% slower.
items.angle: Whatever your priors, credible forecasters putting full automation of AI R&D within about 13 months is the tail scenario that justifies the AI capex the market is currently de-rating.
items.tweetA: A well-regarded forecasting group puts a superhuman AI researcher at August 2027, nine months away. The market is pricing NVDA at under 10x forward earnings. Both can't be right.
items.tweetB: If AI R&D is fully automated by end-2027, today's compute buildout is too small, not too big. The AI bear case requires these forecasts to be very wrong. Size your position by how wrong you think they are.

items.title: The China math: the US has a ~10x compute edge, so a 20% cap still leaves 2x China's capabilities compute
items.idea: AI Futures argues that if the US has a ~10x compute advantage over Chinese companies, a 20% capabilities cap still leaves US labs with at least twice China's capabilities R&D compute. They also argue lab security is too weak to stop Chinese theft (below RAND's OC4/OC5 levels), so racing gives a smaller lead than assumed. The plan is net-negative only if near-term AI risk is low and China doesn't steal.
items.angle: The 'race with China' justification for unlimited AI capex weakens if the lead is huge and leaky. Combined with Rubio's hawkishness, export control, not compute caps, looks like the likelier US policy lever.
items.tweetA: The US has ~10x China's AI compute. Cap capabilities R&D at 20% and the US still has 2x. Unless China steals the weights, and US lab security says it probably can. The race argument depends on security, not speed.
items.tweetB: Weak lab security means every algorithmic breakthrough is a gift to whoever steals it. Spending to move faster without spending to secure it is subsidizing the rival.

items.title: Algorithmic progress at 3-30x a year vs compute at ~5x: why caps create a dangerous 'algorithmic overhang'
items.idea: Estimates of algorithmic progress range from 3x to 30x a year, possibly faster recently, against about 5x a year for compute. Limiting training without limiting algorithmic R&D creates an overhang that, once released, produces a discontinuous capability jump. Leakage means unused algorithms still help trailing actors. Alternatives considered include internal deployment lags and 'researcher holidays'.
items.angle: If algorithms improve faster than compute, compute efficiency gains eventually compress hardware demand per unit of capability. That's the DeepSeek-style risk for the AI-infra trade, offset by Jevons demand.
items.tweetA: Algorithms improving 3-30x a year, compute 5x a year. If the high end is right, software is outrunning hardware by up to 6x. That's great for AI progress and an open question for anyone pricing $NVDA on compute scarcity.
items.tweetB: Pausing training doesn't pause progress. It banks it. When the pause ends, the jump is discontinuous. Every AI regulation built on training thresholds has this flaw.

items.title: Lead sizes: the US top 2 labs are ~3 months ahead, the top 5 ~6 months. SB 53 lying penalty is at most $1M
items.idea: AI Futures estimates the US top 2 labs (OpenAI, Anthropic) have a ~3-month lead over everyone else, and the top 5 (adding Meta, GDM, xAI) about 6 months. Current SB 53 framework violations carry a fine of at most $1M, which is why they push for disclosure in financial filings, where lying exposes executives to criminal liability and investor lawsuits.
items.angle: A 3-month lead is a thin moat for $100B+ valuations. And moving AI-safety disclosure into securities law turns it into a shareholder-litigation risk, a new governance overhang for newly public labs.
items.tweetA: The two leading AI labs are about 3 months ahead of everyone else. Three months. A frontier lab's moat is roughly one quarter of R&D, and investors are pricing it like a decade.
items.tweetB: California's penalty for lying about AI safety: at most $1M. The SEC's penalty: prison. Safety disclosure becomes real when it moves into the 10-K. Newly public AI labs should expect it.
